{{Short description|Abstract algebra polynominal in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], in the realm of [[abstract algebra]], a '''radical polynomial''' is a multivariate [[polynomial]]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Barbeau |first=E. J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CynRMm5qTmQC |title=Polynomials |date=2003-10-09 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-0-387-40627-5 |language=en}}</ref> over a field that can be expressed as a polynomial in the sum of squares of the variables. That is, if 

:<math>k[x_1, x_2,\ldots, x_n]</math> 

is a [[polynomial ring]], the ring of radical polynomials is the subring generated by the polynomial<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sethuraman |first=B. A. |url=http://archive.org/details/ringsfieldsvecto0000seth |title=Rings, fields, and vector spaces : an introduction to abstract algebra via geometric constructability |date=1997 |publisher=New York : Springer |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-387-94848-5}}</ref> 

:<math>\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2.</math>

Radical polynomials are characterized as precisely those polynomials that are [[invariant (mathematics)|invariant]] under the action of the [[orthogonal group]].

The ring of radical polynomials is a [[graded algebra|graded subalgebra]] of the ring of all polynomials.

The standard [[separation of variables theorem]] asserts that every polynomial can be expressed as a finite sum of terms, each term being a product of a radical polynomial and a [[harmonic polynomial]]. This is equivalent to the statement that the ring of all polynomials is a [[free module]] over the ring of radical polynomials.
